title: How photosynthesis works
summary: See how plants turn air, water, and sunlight into their own food, and why that gives us oxygen.
objective: Explain what a plant takes in and gives out during photosynthesis, and predict what happens when light, water, or carbon dioxide is missing.

hook.prompt: A giant oak tree grows from a tiny acorn. Where does most of the solid stuff in its wood come from?

options.text: The soil
options.feedback: It's the most common guess, but soil only supplies small amounts of minerals. The pot of soil barely gets lighter as a tree grows.

options.text: Water from the roots
options.feedback: Water is part of it, but it isn't where most of the solid wood comes from.

options.text: The air
Sunlight
options.feedback: Sunlight powers the process, but light isn't a material a tree can be built from.

hook.explanation: Surprisingly, most of a tree's solid mass is pulled out of thin air. Photosynthesis is how it does that.

bricks.title: The recipe
bricks.body: **Photosynthesis** is how plants make their own food. A plant takes in **carbon dioxide** from the air through tiny holes in its leaves, and **water** from the soil through its roots. **Sunlight** gives the energy to join them into **sugar**, the plant's food. **Oxygen** is left over, and the plant lets it out into the air. Light is only the power: it doesn't become part of the sugar.

term.definition: How plants use the energy in light to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar, giving off oxygen.

visual.alt: A flow: carbon dioxide from the air, water from the roots, and sunlight as energy go into the leaf; sugar and oxygen come out.

bricks.prompt: Sort each one: does it go into photosynthesis, or come out of it?
bricks.hint: Two ingredients and one source of energy go in.
bricks.explanation: Carbon dioxide and water are the ingredients and sunlight is the energy. Sugar is the food made, and oxygen is the leftover.

bricks.prompt: A plant gets plenty of sunlight and air, but its soil has completely dried out. Can it keep making sugar?

options.text: No, because water is one of the ingredients
Yes, it can make sugar from carbon dioxide and light alone
options.feedback: Light is only the energy. With carbon dioxide as the only ingredient, half the recipe is missing.

options.text: Yes, its leaves take in the water it needs from the air
options.feedback: Leaves take in carbon dioxide. The water comes up from the soil through the roots.

bricks.hint: Check the recipe: what comes in through the roots?
bricks.explanation: Sugar needs both carbon dioxide and water. With dry soil, the roots have no water to send up, so sugar-making stalls.

bricks.title: Chlorophyll catches the light
bricks.body: The work happens inside leaf cells, in tiny green parts called **chloroplasts**. They're packed with **chlorophyll**, a green substance that soaks up light. Chlorophyll absorbs mostly **red and blue** light and bounces **green** light back, which is why leaves look green. Green parts like leaves do almost all the photosynthesis. No light, no energy: in the dark, sugar-making stops.

term.definition: The green substance in plant cells that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.

bricks.prompt: Why do most leaves look green to us?

options.text: Chlorophyll bounces green light back instead of absorbing it
Chlorophyll absorbs green light better than any other color
options.feedback: It's the reverse. The color you see is the light that bounces back to your eyes, not the light that's soaked up.

options.text: The sugar inside the leaf is green
options.feedback: The color comes from chlorophyll, the substance that catches light, not from the sugar the leaf makes.

bricks.hint: Which colors does chlorophyll soak up, and which does it send back?
bricks.explanation: Chlorophyll soaks up red and blue light and bounces green back to our eyes, so leaves look green.

bricks.prompt: Which part of a carrot plant does almost none of its photosynthesis?

options.text: The orange root underground
The green leafy top
options.feedback: The leafy top is green and sits in the sun, so that's where the carrot plant makes its sugar.

bricks.hint: Photosynthesis needs green chlorophyll and light. Which part has neither?
bricks.explanation: The root isn't green and sits in the dark soil, so it can't catch light. The green leaves above ground do the work.

bricks.title: Sugar builds the plant
bricks.body: The sugar is the plant's food. Some of it is broken down for **energy** to grow and stay alive. The rest becomes the **building material** for new leaves, stems, roots, and wood. That's how a tree grows heavy: most of its solid mass started as **carbon dioxide** from the air. The oxygen it lets out is part of the air we breathe.

bricks.prompt: What does a plant do with the sugar it makes?

options.text: Breaks some of it down for energy to grow and stay alive
Uses it to build new leaves, stems, and roots
Lets it out into the air through its leaves
options.feedback: That's the oxygen. The sugar stays inside the plant as its food and building material.

options.text: Sends it down to the roots to feed the soil
options.feedback: The plant keeps its sugar for itself: it's the plant's own food, not food for the soil.

bricks.hint: The sugar is food. What do living things use food for?
bricks.explanation: Sugar is both fuel and building material: some gives energy, the rest becomes the plant's body.

bricks.prompt: People plant forests to take carbon dioxide out of the air. How do growing trees do that?

options.text: They turn it into sugar, and then into wood that stays in the tree
They suck it in through their roots and store it in the soil
options.feedback: Roots take in water. Carbon dioxide enters through the tiny holes in the leaves.

options.text: They swap it for oxygen, and nothing else is left behind
options.feedback: Oxygen is only the leftover. The carbon dioxide becomes sugar, and much of that sugar becomes the tree's wood.

bricks.hint: Follow the carbon dioxide: what is it turned into, and where does that end up?
bricks.explanation: Carbon dioxide becomes sugar, and sugar becomes wood. As long as the tree keeps growing, that wood holds on to it.

challenge.prompt: A potted plant is sealed inside a glass jar with moist soil and left in bright sunlight all afternoon. What happens inside the jar?

options.text: The amount of carbon dioxide in the air goes down
The amount of oxygen in the air goes up
The soil gets noticeably lighter, because the plant is built from it
options.feedback: The plant's new material comes mostly from carbon dioxide in the air, not from the soil.

options.text: Nothing changes, because sealing the jar stops photosynthesis
options.feedback: The jar still holds light, water, and air with carbon dioxide in it, so the plant keeps making sugar for now.

challenge.hint: Check the recipe: what goes in, and what comes out?
challenge.explanation: With light and water, the plant keeps taking carbon dioxide out of the jar's air to make sugar, and lets oxygen out as the leftover.

takeaways: Plants use energy from light to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar, giving off oxygen.
Chlorophyll in green parts like leaves catches the light, so no light means no sugar.
The sugar is the plant's fuel and building material, so most of a plant's mass comes from the air.
